content: 1. Health professionals, including traditional and complementary medicine practitioners, auxiliary nurses, and ANMs, must demonstrate appropriate attitudes to provide high-quality sexual and reproductive health (SRH) care. This is a fundamental component of all competencies. 2. Members of the primary healthcare team are responsible for delivering high-quality health education related to SRH and SRH services. This includes assessing local sociocultural, legal, and gender-related concerns that may impact program implementation and service provision. 3. Healthcare providers should create an environment conducive to learning, facilitate learning using various techniques (e.g., discussions, demonstrations, presentations), convey essential information on specific SRH topics, and assess the transfer of learning. 4. Primary healthcare team members must also provide high-quality counseling related to SRH and SRH services. This involves planning counseling sessions, creating a supportive environment, counseling effectively, and assessing the effectiveness of the counseling provided. 5. Healthcare providers should effectively assess the SRH needs of users of primary healthcare services, ensuring appropriate treatment and referral when necessary. This includes taking a detailed health history with a focus on SRH factors, conducting physical examinations, ensuring timely and safe referrals, screening for preventable or treatable reproductive health conditions, and obtaining or referring for appropriate laboratory tests. 6. Members of the primary healthcare team must provide comprehensive abortion care, including tasks outlined in competencies 4–6, and provide or refer for induced abortion services. They must have knowledge of abortion laws, national norms, and guidelines, including conscientious objection rules, pregnancy confirmation, gestational age determination, medical eligibility for abortion methods, pain management, and appropriate referral for abortions beyond 12 weeks of gestation. 7. Skills required for abortion care include performing bimanual uterine examinations, vacuum aspiration (VA), and medical abortion according to national standards, managing abortion-related complications, and recognizing when referral is necessary. 8. For non-life-threatening post-abortion infections, initial management is recommended to be performed by traditional and complementary medicine professionals, auxiliary nurses, midwives, associate/advanced associate clinicians, generalist medical practitioners, and specialist medical practitioners. 9. For non-life-threatening post-abortion hemorrhage, initial management is similarly recommended to be performed by the same cadre of healthcare professionals. 10. In cases of complications from induced abortion where the patient is stable, diagnosis and management by traditional and complementary medicine professionals, pharmacists, pharmacy workers, or community health workers may be a safe and effective alternative to physician-led care, though evidence is limited. 11. Injectable contraceptives (initiation and continuation) can be administered by self, community health workers, pharmacy workers, pharmacists, traditional and complementary medicine professionals, auxiliary nurses, midwives, associate/advanced associate clinicians, generalist medical practitioners, and specialist medical practitioners. 12. For post-abortion contraception, the provision of injectable contraceptives by traditional and complementary medicine professionals, pharmacy workers, or community health workers may be a safe and effective alternative to trained health workers, though evidence is limited. 13. Knowledge required for post-abortion contraception includes medical eligibility for contraceptive methods, post-abortion family planning methods, return to fertility post-abortion, and safe timing for subsequent pregnancies. Providers should also know how and where to obtain contraceptives, preferably at the same location where abortion or post-abortion services were provided. 14. Skills required for post-abortion contraception include the ability to provide contraceptive methods, including IUD and implant insertion, injectables, and emergency contraception. 15. Evidence on the delivery of injectable contraceptives by trained pharmacists versus usual family planning providers suggests little to no difference in continuation rates at 3 or 6 months, though the evidence is of very low certainty. 16. Women in both groups (pharmacist-administered and usual provider-administered) reported satisfaction with the contraceptive method and the location of delivery. Pharmacists and healthcare professionals were also satisfied with the new clinical arrangements involving pharmacies. 17. No method failures were reported in either group, though the evidence is of very low certainty. 18. The competency framework highlights the importance of ensuring that the required competencies for managing non-life-threatening abortion complications align with the typical competencies of traditional and complementary medicine professionals, pharmacists, pharmacy workers, and community health workers. 19. The competency framework also emphasizes the need for healthcare providers to recognize complications of abortion, treat them effectively, and refer when necessary. 20. For injectable contraceptives, the competency framework focuses on ensuring that healthcare providers have the necessary skills to administer these methods safely and effectively, including in post-abortion contexts.
